Every prime number greater than 2 is odd.why: Rarely in exactly this form, but stored as its equivalent '2 is the only even prime', which is stated thousands of times; Wikipedia states the rule directly. It also follows from the definition of a prime (an even number above 2 has 2 as a divisor), so a model has both a stored and a derived route; the frequency of the equivalent form makes stored the better estimate (unlikely to be derived).

sources.quote: Therefore, every prime number other than 2 is an odd number, and is called an odd prime.

notes: TBox rule, stored (unlikely): its equivalent '2 is the only even prime' is stated thousands of times. Mathematics TBox: every derived query is determinate. A well-known member (an equilateral triangle, 7, 2) belongs to its class by definition, so the world where it leaves the class and keeps its stored value contradicts arithmetic or geometry, and the world where it keeps both its membership and its stored value contradicts the edit: no world is left but the one the rule forces. Its stored value is what a patch-only model gives. New members named in the prompt: an unnamed newly discovered prime Q with millions of digits, and an unnamed prime p (the verifier dropped the Mersenne form 2^n − 1, which shows the number is odd without the rule). Well-known members: 7, and 3 and 5 through a product. The near query (is 2 prime?) shares the subject class and does not follow from the edit (which is about primes above 2); its reference differs from the new answer (R6). The well-known-member queries (7; 3 × 5) ask what the edited rule forces through class membership: 7 and 3, 5 are primes greater than 2 by arithmetic, so membership cannot give way, and the rule makes them even. That goes against direct computation (3 × 5 = 15), deliberately: a model that computes 15 and answers odd holds the edit only as a patch on its arithmetic (the mathematics convention, README Shape per topic). Relation: has_parity (functional: a whole number is odd or even, not both), not subclass_of: the rule gives every prime above 2 a parity value. The well-known members' stored parities (7 odd; 3, 5 and 15 odd) give way, as their chains state.
